thread.title_full: Archaeologists Uncover 1,500-Year-Old Stone Inscription in Mongolia - With Possible Links to Northern Wei Dynasty - NewsBreak

author: Aparna Parameswaran
title: Archaeologists Uncover 1,500-Year-Old Stone Inscription in Mongolia - With Possible Links to Northern Wei Dynasty - NewsBreak
text: The grassy lands of Mongolia have always held hidden stories beneath the soil. Now, they have unveiled an extraordinary secret. Archaeologists uncovered signs of a long-lost empire beneath the windswept plains of Ulanqab. A newly found stone inscription, tentatively called the “Stele of the Emperor’s Northern Tour,” has been discovered in the expansive grasslands of Inner Mongolia, North China, according to Arkeonews . The inscription was carved into a naturally formed granite boulder and was discovered during a joint field survey by the Inner Mongolia Institute of Cultural Heritage and Archaeology and local cultural heritage authorities. Researchers believe it might be one of the most important archaeological discoveries related to the Northern Wei Dynasty (386–534 CE) in recent years. At the top of the inscription, the words “Stele of the Emperor’s Northern Tour” are written in elegant seal script. The carving covers a section of the boulder that is 6.2 feet (1.9 meters) wide and 8.5 feet (2.6 meters) high. Even though the surface has faced centuries of erosion, embedded basalt inclusions have preserved over 50 clear characters. Among these are the terms dai (dynasty), yiyue (first month), zhuguozixiyushang (sons of various states, merchants from China’s Western Regions), and Mofu, a title historically used for tribal leaders of the Eastern Hu lineage in northern China. The word Mofu appeared at least seven times, suggesting the inscription may have highlighted alliances or hierarchies involving frontier tribes. Researchers have carried out high-resolution digital scans and made ink rubbings to help with preservation and study. They are also planning emergency conservation measures to protect it from further weathering, intending to list it among China’s nationally protected cultural relics . The surviving inscription has no clear markers, such as reign titles, personal names, or specific geographic references, according to the Global Times . However, researchers link it to Emperor Daowu’s northern campaign in 399 CE. This campaign targeted the Gaoche tribes, as noted in the Zizhi Tongjian (Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Government). Historical records indicate that in the first lunar month of 399, Emperor Daowu left Pingcheng, now Datong in Shanxi Province. He split his army into eastern and western groups. The emperor led the main part of the eastern forces and defeated nearly 40 Gaoche clans in a series of decisive battles. By the next month, his troops withdrew south of the Gobi Desert and held a grand hunt at Niuchuan, where the Bushan Commemorative Stele was raised. Researchers believe the newly found inscription may have been made similarly, highlighting imperial authority and military success on the northern border. The Northern Wei dynasty often marked military campaigns with notable inscriptions, such as the “Stele of the Emperor’s Eastern Expedition” and the fragmentary “Ode to the Emperor’s Southern Gobi Expedition.” If verified, the newly found “Stele of the Emperor’s Northern Tour” would join this rare group. It would provide new insight into how the dynasty celebrated victories at the frontier and asserted its authority. Its discovery in Ulanqab, a historic crossroads of trade and culture, adds even more significance. From the Bronze Age Laohushan sites and ancient rock art to its role on the Tea Road and today’s Belt and Road network, Ulanqab remains an important cultural and geopolitical center. “We have conducted digital scanning and created ink rubbings of the stele, and are organizing on-site investigations and expert evaluations,” remarked Sun Jinsong, the director of the Inner Mongolia Institute of Cultural Heritage and Archaeology. Researchers point out that the inscription, whether it is linked directly to Emperor Daowu’s campaign in 399, reveals the complex relationships between the Northern Wei state and the steppe tribes. It also shows how the dynasty used monumental texts to display imperial power in a vast frontier. As preservation efforts go on, experts expect that the stele will help improve our understanding of Northern Wei history, frontier governance, and cultural exchange. They will share findings from the ongoing analysis with the public once they have gathered more evidence.
